fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Precursor to The Core of Adjoint Functors

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Mentioned in passing as 2.1. Proposition., as "well-known".

html:ul.html:li: Suppose U : A → X is a functor, F : X .ob → A .ob a function, and (πₓ : A(F(x), -) ≅ X(x, U(-)))_{x ∈ X} a family of natural isomorphisms. Then there is a unique extension \overline {F} of F such that (πₓ)_{x ∈ X} is natural in x, witnessing \overline {F} ⊣ U.
Or dually, suppose that F is a functor, but U is just a function on objects, and (πₐ : A(F(-), a) ≅ X(-, U(a)))_{a ∈ A}. Then U uniquely extends to \overline {U}.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let's be pedantic and clarify that A(F(-), -), X(-, U(-)): Xᵒᵖ → Setᴬ have the same action on morphisms as Hom(-, -)∘Fᵒᵖ, λx. Hom(x, -)∘U. This is conventionally left implicit, but we remark to clarify what we mean by the family of natural isomorphisms being natural.
NOTE: I couldn't get よ to render in the latex (diagrams). I'm not sure if it's a lualatex/dvi or font issue.

We take inspiration from the thin case. We wts the F-action on morphisms is fully determined already (∃!). That is, we have two goals:
(∃) Show that there is a suitable F-action.
(!) That any other F-action is equal to it.
As usual, let η_x = πₓ(F(x))(1_{F(x)}) : X(x, U∘F(x)) denote the component of the unit of the (a posteriori) adjunction and ϵₐ = π_{U(a)}(a)⁻¹(1_{U(a)}) denote the component of the counit.

html:ul.html:li:
(∃)
Now suppose ∃f : X(x, y). Since η_y : X(y, U∘F(y)), we have η_y∘f : X(x, U∘F(y)). By the Hom bijection, πₓ(F(y))⁻¹(η_y∘f) : A(F(x), F(y)). This is our candidate for the F-action. \overline {F}(f) ≔ πₓ(F(y))⁻¹(η_y ∘ f).
As a picture, each f : X(x, y) gives rise to the following square in Set: Johnson He20245102025927https://hejohns.github.io/forest/subb-000D/subb-000D/forest/subb-000D/
\usepackage {tikz-cd} \usepackage {unicode-math} \begin {tikzcd} A(F(x), F(y)) & A(F(y), F(y)) \ar [d, "≀"', "π_y(F(y))"] \\ X(x, U∘F(y)) \ar [u, "≀"', "πₓ(F(y))⁻¹"] & X(y, U∘F(y)) \ar [l, "-∘f"] \end {tikzcd}
And our candidate \overline {F}(f) is the one we know to exist by chasing 1_{F(y)} around the square.
We could directly try to show that \overline {F} defined as such is indeed functorial--and I have tried--, but it's rather difficult without the clarifying perspective of the Yoneda lemma (no, seriously, although I'm sure one could do it).
It's instructive to try directly, if one hasn't. The problem is that \overline {F}(f) as defined is not obviously the composition of morphisms in any diagram-- how do you reason about the functoriality of πₓ(F(y))⁻¹? Instead, we want to invoke a representation theorem and work with \overline {F}(f) as an explicit composition in some diagram. The solution is to follow the Yoneda principle and pass from reasoning in Set to Setᴬ.
Notice that the above square is moreover natural in the variable F(y). That is, we've actually described the F(y) component of the natural transformation πₓ⁻¹∘(-∘f)∘π_y : A(F(x), -) ⇐ A(F(y), -). As a picture, each f : X(x, y) gives rise to the following square in Setᴬ: Johnson He20245102025927https://hejohns.github.io/forest/sub-000D/sub-000D/forest/sub-000D/
\usepackage {tikz-cd} \usepackage {unicode-math} \begin {tikzcd} A(F(x), -) & A(F(y), -) \ar [d, Rightarrow, "≀"', "π_y"] \\ X(x, U(-)) \ar [u, Rightarrow, "≀"', "πₓ⁻¹"] & X(y, U(-)) \ar [l, Rightarrow, "-∘f"] \end {tikzcd}
We first make the trivial observation that A(F(x), -) and A(F(y), -) are both Yoneda embeddings (we use the "version" where よ : Aᵒᵖ → Setᴬ, ie the Yoneda embedding on Aᵒᵖ), よ(F(x)) and よ(F(y)) respectively.
Then the Yoneda lemma tells us that by specifying an element \overline {F}(f) : A(F(x), F(y)), this fully determines (ie freely extends to) a natural transformation よ(\overline {F}(f)) = (-∘\overline {F}(f)) : よ(F(x)) ⇐ よ(F(y))
Equivalently, the Yoneda principle tells us that an element \overline {F}(f) : A(F(x), F(y)) fully failthfully embeds as a natural transformation よ(\overline {F}(f)) = (-∘\overline {F}(f)) : よ(F(x)) ⇐ よ(F(y))
With this in mind, we notice that by definition, よ(\overline {F}(f)) is exactly the lid to the above Setᴬ square.
\usepackage {tikz-cd} \usepackage {unicode-math} \begin {tikzcd} A(F(x), -) & A(F(y), -) \ar [d, Rightarrow, "≀"', "π_y"]\ar [l, Rightarrow, "-∘\overline {F}(f)"'] \\ X(x, U(-)) \ar [u, Rightarrow, "≀", "πₓ⁻¹"'] & X(y, U(-)) \ar [l, Rightarrow, "-∘f"] \end {tikzcd}
That is, both natural transformations map 1_{F(y)} to the same thing-- \overline {F}{F}(f)-- by definition, thus must be equal by the Yoneda Lemma. (In hindsight, this line of reasoning is quite circumlocutious and you might as well start by saying such a \overline {F} would have to satisfy this square, but I think it's the more obvious starting point without presupposing it exists.) Now that we've represented \overline {F}(f) as an explicit composition, we have enough to tools consider functoriality.
Wts \overline {F} actually defines a functorial action on morphisms for a functor extending F. Indeed, \overline {F}(1ₓ : X(x, x)) = πₓ(F(x))⁻¹(ηₓ∘1ₓ) = πₓ(F(x))⁻¹(ηₓ) = 1_{F(x)} by definition. And suppose ∃g : X(y, z). Then \overline {F}(g∘f : X(x, z)) viewed as a natural transformation gives rise to the following superimposed squares:
\usepackage {tikz-cd} \usepackage {unicode-math} \begin {tikzcd} A(F(x), -) & A(F(y), -) \ar [d, Rightarrow, "π_y"', shift right=2]\ar [l, Rightarrow, "-∘\overline {F}(f)"'] & A(F(z), -) \ar [d, Rightarrow, "π_z"]\ar [l, Rightarrow, "-∘\tilde {F}(g)"']\ar [ll, Rightarrow, "-∘\overline {F}(g∘f)"', bend right] \\ X(x, U(-)) \ar [u, Rightarrow, "≀"', "πₓ⁻¹"] & X(y, U(-)) \ar [l, Rightarrow, "-∘f"]\ar [u, Rightarrow, "π_y⁻¹"', shift right=2] & X(z, U(-)) \ar [l, Rightarrow, "-∘g"]\ar [ll, Rightarrow, "-∘(g∘f)", bend left] \end {tikzcd}
A diagram chase verifies that the diagram indeed commutes, and that よ(\overline {F}(g∘f)) = よ(\overline {F}(f))∘よ(\overline {F}(g)). By the ("going home" direction of the) Yoneda principle, \overline {F}(g∘f) = \overline {F}(f)∘\overline {F}(g). Thus at last, \overline {F} defines a functorial action on X-morphisms.
We should also check that \overline {F} is actually adjoint to U-- ie, that (πₓ)_{x ∈ X} is indeed natural in the variable x as well as a. By great good fortune, by defining \overline {F} st ∀x,y ∈ X. ∀f ∈ X(x, y). Johnson He2024572024821https://hejohns.github.io/forest/subsub-0007/subsub-0007/forest/subsub-0007/
\usepackage {tikz-cd} \usepackage {unicode-math} \begin {tikzcd} A(F(x), -) \ar [d, Rightarrow, "≀", "πₓ"'] & A(F(y), -) \ar [d, Rightarrow, "≀"', "π_y"]\ar [l, Rightarrow, "-∘\overline {F}(f)"'] \\ X(x, U(-)) & X(y, U(-)) \ar [l, Rightarrow, "-∘f"] \end {tikzcd}
it is indeed the case.

(!)
To finish off the result, we wts for any other F' extending F to morphisms st F' ⊣ U, witnessed by π : Xᵒᵖ → Setᴬ, that F' = \overline {F}. This simply follows from the observation that ∀f. naturality of π is exactly this square, and forces よ(F'(f)) = πₓ⁻¹∘(-∘f)∘π_y = よ(\overline {F}(f))

fr:mainmatter.html:p: So this result is really a corollary of the Yoneda lemma. The nlab page is here.

Of course in hindsight, we could've (or even should've) just defined \overline {F} to be よ⁻¹(πₓ⁻¹∘(-∘f)∘π_y) from the get-go, since it's a much more clearly well-behaved definition, but unless you're already sold on the Yoneda principle, I find it a difficult leap without struggling with lower-level objects a bit first. I'm still in training.
This is the perspective taken in the short proof.
However, unlike the thin case, we crucially use the information that U is a functor so the natural transformation squares are well-defined.

html:ul.html:li: functions U : A .ob → X .ob and F : X .ob → A .ob
a family of isomorphisms (π_{x,a} : A(F(x), a) ≅ X(X, U(a)))_{a ∈ A, x ∈ X}

fr:mainmatter.html:p: An adjunction core extends to an adjuction iff ∀a,b ∈ A. ∀x ∈ X. I commutes, and iff ∀x,y ∈ X. a ∈ A. II commutes. The adjunction is unique when it exists.
The original theorem is stated in terms of \mathcal {V}-enriched categories, but we only treat the simple case of Homset-categories here.

We use the same notation and definitions of η, ϵ, \overline {F}, \overline {U} as the explicit proof of the precursor lemma. The definition of \overline {F}, \overline {U} in the short proof presupposes that U is a functor, so we're scrupulous to avoid circularity.
This proof is rather low tech and is lifted straight from the paper. It's also how you'd attack the precursor head-on. The utility is that it holds in enriched categories.

The forward directions are trivial. Suppose (F, U, (π_{a, x})_{a ∈ A, x ∈ X}) extends to \overline {F} ⊣_π \overline {U}. Then I expresses that ∀g : A(a, b). ∀f : A(F(x), a). π_{x, b}(g∘f) = \overline {U}(g)∘π_{a, x}(f). This is exactly the condition that ∀g : A(a, b). π is natural in a at g, which is certainly true of an adjunction. II expresses something similar (dual).
The nontrivial directions are the backward directions.

html:li.html:p: (I) wts I ⟹ \overline {U} is a functor. Suppose ∀a,b ∈ A. ∀x ∈ X. I holds. Then in particular, ∀c ∈ A. I holds at x = U(c).
which when pasted together, tells us magically:

Combined with the earlier proof that \overline {U}(1ₐ) = 1_{\overline {U}(a)} (which just follows by definition), we've shown that \overline {U} defines a functorial action on morphisms. Actually, we saw earlier that I expresses that π is natural in a, so we've met the preconditions of the precursor lemma, thus there is a unique extension \overline {F} st \overline {F} ⊣_π \overline {U}.
There's two ways ways to see the uniqueness situation:

html:ul.html:li: (Going backwards) Since the definitions of \overline {F} and \overline {U} (in the precursor) are not dependent on the other functor, the total adjunction \overline {F} ⊣ \overline {U} is the unique one extending the core by applying the uniqueness result of the precusor to each functor in turn, just knowing the other is a well-defined functor.

html:li.html:p: (II) wts II ⟹ \overline {F} is a functor. This is dual.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: (For V-enriched categories, ) If V is thin, all diagrams commute, thus an adjunction core always determines an adjunction.
Set isn't thin, but 2 is, thus for posets, an adjunction core gives rise to a thin adjunction, as remarked here. I don't know how useful this lemma is for ordinary Homset categories.

Of course in hindsight, we could've (or even should've) just defined \overline {F} to be よ⁻¹(πₓ⁻¹∘(-∘f)∘π_y) from the get-go, since it's a much more clearly well-behaved definition, but unless you're already sold on the Yoneda principle, I find it a difficult leap without struggling with lower-level objects a bit first. I'm still in training.
This is the perspective taken in the short proof.
